title: Traditional Indian Diet and Daily Walks Put 61% of Early Diabetes Patients in Remission, Study Finds
excerpt: In a 87-person Maharashtra trial, a moderate-carbohydrate diet of everyday Indian foods plus a 40-minute daily walk produced an estimated 60.9% remission rate at six months — with walking consistency the strongest predictor. The researchers caution it was a single-arm study and no one should change medication without a doctor.
body:
• A six-month programme of a traditional Indian diet and daily walking put an estimated 60.9% of adults with early Type 2 diabetes into remission without glucose-lowering medication, a peer-reviewed Indian study found.
  • Participants ate familiar foods — multigrain chapatis, lentils, sprouts, leafy vegetables, nuts and fruit in measured portions, roughly 1,200 kcal a day — and walked 40 minutes daily; average HbA1c fell from 7.32% to 6.27% and average weight by 4.67 kg.
  • Walking adherence mattered most: participants who kept the routine on at least 80% of days had 8.24 times the adjusted odds of remission.
  • The study had no control group and its authors call the findings hypothesis-generating — do not stop or change diabetes medication without your doctor, the researchers stress.

Early Type 2 diabetes can be pushed into remission with ordinary Indian food and a daily walk — no special products, no fasting windows, no skipped meals. That is the finding of a study of 87 adults in Maharashtra, published in Diabetes and Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Research and Reviews, in which a six-month intervention built on a traditional Indian diet and structured walking produced an estimated remission rate of 60.9%.

The study, registered with the Clinical Trial Registry of India and summarised on PubMed, enrolled adults whose diabetes had been diagnosed within the previous two years, at two centres in Pune and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Seventy-five participants completed the six months. Remission was defined strictly: an HbA1c below 6.5%, measured at least three months after stopping glucose-lowering medication.

What participants actually did

The intervention used a Local Healthy Moderate Carbohydrate (LHMC) diet — familiar Indian foods such as multigrain chapatis, lentils, sprouts, green leafy vegetables, nuts and fruits in measured portions — at roughly 1,200 kcal a day, a reduction of about 500 kcal from baseline. Alongside it came daily structured exercise: a 40-minute walk and 10 minutes of deep breathing, as the researchers described the programme to The Indian Express. Dr Vedavati Purandare, consultant diabetologist and head of clinical services at Chellaram Hospital's diabetes care centre, made the point that participants did not need special foods, skipped meals or fasting windows.

The results, in absolute terms: of the 87 adults who started, the researchers estimated a 60.9% remission rate at six months. Average HbA1c fell from 7.32% to 6.27% — a drop of just over one percentage point — and average body weight fell by 4.67 kg. The strongest signal was not the menu but the routine: participants who followed the walking prescription on at least 80% of days had 8.24 times the adjusted odds of achieving remission compared with those who walked less consistently.

The caveats, stated plainly

This was a single-arm study: everyone received the intervention, and there was no comparison group eating or walking differently. The authors state that the absence of a comparator limits causal inference and that the findings are hypothesis-generating, warranting confirmation in controlled trials. Dr A G Unnikrishnan, CEO and endocrinologist at Chellaram Hospital, told The Indian Express that the findings showed early diabetes could be put into remission through dietary and lifestyle change, and added two cautions: larger controlled trials are needed, and patients should change their treatment only after consulting their doctors.

What this means for you

For diaspora readers managing early Type 2 diabetes — a condition that strikes South Asians earlier and at lower body weights than most populations — the study's practical message is narrow but useful. The window matters: everyone in the trial was within two years of diagnosis. The food was culturally ordinary, which is precisely why the authors argue the approach is scalable. And the deciding factor was adherence to a daily 40-minute walk. If you are within that early window, this is a study worth raising with your own doctor — not a reason to stop medication on your own.
